\section{Overview}

Declarations of the Lean module \texttt{TCSlib.Programs.Light.Lib.Seg}.

\section{Declarations}

\begin{definition}[Memory segment representation]
\lean{Light.Seg}
\label{Light.Seg}
\leanok
For a memory function $\mu:\mathbb{N}\to\mathbb{Z}$, a starting address $a$, and a list
$l$ of integers, say that $l$ is represented in memory at $a$ when every valid index $i$
into $l$ satisfies $\mu(a+i)=l[i]$.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Reading a memory segment]
\lean{Light.readSeg}
\label{Light.readSeg}
\leanok
Given a memory function $\mu:\mathbb{N}\to\mathbb{Z}$, a starting address $a$, and a
length $n$, the list read from that segment is the sequence
$\mu(a),\mu(a+1),\ldots,\mu(a+n-1)$.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Length of a read segment]
\lean{Light.length_readSeg}
\label{Light.length_readSeg}
\leanok
\uses{Light.readSeg}
\difficulty{1}
For every function $\mu:\mathbb N\to\mathbb Z$ and natural numbers $a,n$, the list of
values $\mu(a+i)$ for $i=0,\ldots,n-1$ has length $n$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Entries of a read segment]
\lean{Light.getElem_readSeg}
\label{Light.getElem_readSeg}
\leanok
\uses{Light.readSeg}
\difficulty{1}
Let $\mu:\mathbb N\to\mathbb Z$ and $a,n\in\mathbb N$. For any index $i$ less than the
length of the list whose entries are $\mu(a),\mu(a+1),\ldots,\mu(a+n-1)$, the entry at
index $i$ is $\mu(a+i)$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Entries of a read segment]
\lean{Light.getD_readSeg}
\label{Light.getD_readSeg}
\leanok
\uses{Light.getElem_readSeg, Light.readSeg}
\difficulty{3}
Let $\mu:\mathbb N\to\mathbb Z$, and let $a,n,i\in\mathbb N$ with $i<n$. The entry at
index $i$ of the length-$n$ list of values $\mu(a),\mu(a+1),\ldots,\mu(a+n-1)$ is
$\mu(a+i)$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[A sequence segment read from a function]
\lean{Light.seg_readSeg}
\label{Light.seg_readSeg}
\leanok
\uses{Light.Seg, Light.readSeg}
\difficulty{1}
Let $\mu:\mathbb{N}\to\mathbb{Z}$, and let $a,n\in\mathbb{N}$. The values of $\mu$
starting at index $a$ agree, at every index in the list, with the list of the first $n$
values $\mu(a),\mu(a+1),\ldots,\mu(a+n-1)$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[The empty list is a segment]
\lean{Light.Seg.nil}
\label{Light.Seg.nil}
\leanok
\uses{Light.Seg}
\difficulty{1}
For every function $\mu:\mathbb{N}\to\mathbb{Z}$ and every $a\in\mathbb{N}$, the empty
list is a segment of the values of $\mu$ starting at $a$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Values within a segment]
\lean{Light.Seg.get}
\label{Light.Seg.get}
\leanok
\uses{Light.Seg}
\difficulty{1}
Let $\mu:\mathbb{N}\to\mathbb{Z}$, let $a\in\mathbb{N}$, and let $l$ be a finite list of
integers whose entries are the values of $\mu$ starting at $a$. For every index $i$ less
than the length of $l$, the value $\mu(a+i)$ equals the $i$th entry of $l$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Defaulted list lookup within a segment]
\lean{Light.Seg.getD}
\label{Light.Seg.getD}
\leanok
\uses{Light.Seg}
\difficulty{3}
Let $\mu:\mathbb{N}\to\mathbb{Z}$, let $a\in\mathbb{N}$, and let $l$ be a finite list of
integers whose entries are the values of $\mu$ starting at $a$. For every index $i$ less
than the length of $l$ and every integer $d$, the value $\mu(a+i)$ equals the list
lookup at index $i$ with default value $d$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Recovering a segment by reading values]
\lean{Light.Seg.eq_readSeg}
\label{Light.Seg.eq_readSeg}
\leanok
\uses{Light.Seg, Light.getElem_readSeg, Light.readSeg}
\difficulty{4}
Let $\mu:\mathbb{N}\to\mathbb{Z}$, let $a\in\mathbb{N}$, and let $l$ be a finite list of
integers whose entries are the values of $\mu$ starting at $a$. Then $l$ is exactly the
list of values $\mu(a),\mu(a+1),\ldots,\mu(a+|l|-1)$, where $|l|$ denotes the length of
$l$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Characterization of a sequence segment]
\lean{Light.seg_cons}
\label{Light.seg_cons}
\leanok
\uses{Light.Seg}
\difficulty{4}
Let $\mu:\mathbb{N}\to\mathbb{Z}$, let $a\in\mathbb{N}$, and let $x\in\mathbb{Z}$ and
$l$ be a finite list of integers. The values of $\mu$ starting at index $a$ agree with
the list obtained by placing $x$ before $l$ if and only if $\mu(a)=x$ and the values
starting at index $a+1$ agree with $l$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Segments over concatenated lists]
\lean{Light.seg_append}
\label{Light.seg_append}
\leanok
\uses{Light.Seg}
\difficulty{5}
Let $\mu$ map natural numbers to integers, let $a$ be a natural number, and let
$l_1,l_2$ be lists of integers. The memory segment beginning at $a$ agrees with the
concatenation $l_1++l_2$ if and only if it agrees with $l_1$ beginning at $a$ and with
$l_2$ beginning at $a+|l_1|$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Taking an initial segment]
\lean{Light.Seg.take}
\label{Light.Seg.take}
\leanok
\uses{Light.Seg}
\difficulty{3}
Let $\mu : \mathbb{N}\to\mathbb{Z}$, let $a\in\mathbb{N}$, let $l$ be a finite list of
integers, and let $k\in\mathbb{N}$. If $\mu(a+i)=l_i$ for every index $i<|l|$, then
$\mu(a+i)=(l\mathbin{\mathrm{take}}k)_i$ for every index in the list formed by taking
the first $k$ entries of $l$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Dropping the initial segment]
\lean{Light.Seg.drop}
\label{Light.Seg.drop}
\leanok
\uses{Light.Seg}
\difficulty{3}
Let $\mu:\mathbb{N}\to\mathbb{Z}$, let $a,k\in\mathbb{N}$, and let $l$ be a finite list
of integers. If the entries of $l$ give the values of $\mu$ starting at $a$, then the
list obtained by dropping the first $k$ entries gives the values of $\mu$ starting at
$a+k$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Agreement preserves a segment]
\lean{Light.Seg.congr}
\label{Light.Seg.congr}
\leanok
\uses{Light.Seg}
\difficulty{3}
Let $\mu,\mu':\mathbb{N}\to\mathbb{Z}$, let $a\in\mathbb{N}$, and let $l$ be a finite
list of integers. If $\mu(a+i)$ equals the $i$th entry of $l$ for every index $i$ within
the list, and $\mu'(a+i)=\mu(a+i)$ for every such index, then $\mu'(a+i)$ also equals
the $i$th entry of $l$ throughout the list.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Preserving a segment under agreement]
\lean{Light.Seg.keep}
\label{Light.Seg.keep}
\leanok
\uses{Light.Inside, Light.SameOn, Light.Seg, Light.Seg.congr}
\difficulty{3}
Let $\mu,\mu':\mathbb{N}\to\mathbb{Z}$, let $a\in\mathbb{N}$, and let $l$ be a finite
list of integers whose entries are the values of $\mu$ starting at $a$. If $\mu'$ agrees
with $\mu$ at every index $j$ satisfying $a\le j<a+|l|$, then the entries of $l$ are
also the values of $\mu'$ starting at $a$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Updating a value inside a segment]
\lean{Light.Seg.update_in}
\label{Light.Seg.update_in}
\leanok
\uses{Light.Seg}
\difficulty{4}
Let $\mu : \mathbb{N}\to\mathbb{Z}$, let $a\in\mathbb{N}$, and let $l$ be a finite list
of integers. Suppose $\mu(a+j)=l_j$ for every index $j<|l|$. For any index $i<|l|$ and
integer $x$, changing $\mu(a+i)$ to $x$ makes the resulting function agree, starting at
$a$, with the list obtained by replacing the entry $l_i$ by $x$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Updating a value outside a segment]
\lean{Light.Seg.update_out}
\label{Light.Seg.update_out}
\leanok
\uses{Light.Seg, Light.Seg.congr}
\difficulty{3}
Let $\mu : \mathbb{N}\to\mathbb{Z}$, let $a,b\in\mathbb{N}$, and let $l$ be a finite
list of integers. Suppose $\mu(a+i)=l_i$ for every index $i<|l|$. If $b<a$ or $a+|l|\le
b$, then changing the value of $\mu$ at $b$ to any integer leaves these values on the
segment from $a$ unchanged.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Appending a value to a segment]
\lean{Light.Seg.snoc}
\label{Light.Seg.snoc}
\leanok
\uses{Light.Seg, Light.Seg.update_out, Light.seg_append, Light.seg_cons}
\difficulty{3}
Let $\mu : \mathbb{N}\to\mathbb{Z}$, let $a\in\mathbb{N}$, and let $l$ be a finite list
of integers. If $\mu(a+i)=l_i$ for every index $i<|l|$, then changing the value of $\mu$
at $a+|l|$ to an integer $x$ makes it agree with the list obtained by appending $x$ to
$l$, at every index starting at $a$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Agreement on a finite segment]
\lean{Light.Seg.of_sameOn}
\label{Light.Seg.of_sameOn}
\leanok
\uses{Light.SameOn, Light.Seg, Light.Seg.congr}
\difficulty{3}
Let $\mu,\mu' : \mathbb{N}\to\mathbb{Z}$, let $b\in\mathbb{N}$, and let $l$ be a finite
list of integers. Suppose that $\mu'$ agrees with $\mu$ at every natural number
satisfying a predicate $K$, and that $K(b+i)$ holds for every index $i<|l|$. If
$\mu(b+i)=l_i$ for every such index, then $\mu'(b+i)=l_i$ for every such index.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Reflexivity outside an interval]
\lean{Light.SameOutside.refl}
\label{Light.SameOutside.refl}
\leanok
\uses{Light.SameOn.refl, Light.SameOutside}
\difficulty{1}
For any integer-valued sequence $\mu$ and natural numbers $a,n$, the sequence agrees
with itself at every index less than $a$ or at least $a+n$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Monotonicity outside an interval]
\lean{Light.SameOutside.mono}
\label{Light.SameOutside.mono}
\leanok
\uses{Light.SameOutside}
\difficulty{2}
Let $\mu,\mu'$ be integer-valued sequences and let $a,n,a',n'$ be natural numbers.
Suppose they agree at every index less than $a$ or at least $a+n$, with $a'\le a$ and
$a+n\le a'+n'$. Then they agree at every index less than $a'$ or at least $a'+n'$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Updating inside an interval]
\lean{Light.SameOutside.update}
\label{Light.SameOutside.update}
\leanok
\uses{Light.SameOutside}
\difficulty{3}
Let $\mu,\mu'$ be integer-valued sequences and let $a,n,b$ be natural numbers. Suppose
they agree at every index less than $a$ or at least $a+n$, and suppose $a\le b<a+n$. For
every integer $x$, replacing the value of $\mu'$ at $b$ by $x$ preserves agreement with
$\mu$ at every index less than $a$ or at least $a+n$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Reflexivity outside two intervals]
\lean{Light.SameOutside2.refl}
\label{Light.SameOutside2.refl}
\leanok
\uses{Light.SameOn.refl, Light.SameOutside2}
\difficulty{1}
For any integer-valued sequence $\mu$ and natural numbers $a,n,b,m$, the sequence agrees
with itself at every index that is either less than $a$ or at least $a+n$, and also
either less than $b$ or at least $b+m$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Preservation under an interior update]
\lean{Light.SameOutside2.update}
\label{Light.SameOutside2.update}
\leanok
\uses{Light.SameOn.write, Light.SameOutside2}
\difficulty{2}
Let $\mu,\mu':\mathbb{N}\to\mathbb{Z}$ and let $a,n,b,m,c\in\mathbb{N}$. Suppose $\mu$
and $\mu'$ agree at every natural number that lies outside both intervals $[a,a+n)$ and
$[b,b+m)$, and suppose $c$ lies in at least one of those intervals. Then replacing the
value of $\mu'$ at $c$ by any integer $x$ preserves its agreement with $\mu$ outside
both intervals.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Agreement outside a segment]
\lean{Light.Seg.of_sameOutside}
\label{Light.Seg.of_sameOutside}
\leanok
\uses{Light.SameOutside, Light.Seg, Light.Seg.congr}
\difficulty{3}
Let $\mu,\mu' : \mathbb{N}\to\mathbb{Z}$, let $a,b,n\in\mathbb{N}$, and let $l$ be a
finite list of integers. Suppose $\mu'$ agrees with $\mu$ at every natural number
outside the interval $[a,a+n)$, meaning at every $c<a$ or $a+n\le c$. Suppose also that
$\mu(b+i)=l_i$ for every index $i<|l|$, and that the segment from $b$ through $b+|l|-1$
lies entirely before that interval or entirely at or after its endpoint: $b+|l|\le a$ or
$a+n\le b$. Then $\mu'(b+i)=l_i$ for every index $i<|l|$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{definition}[Natural-valued memory segment]
\lean{Light.SegN}
\label{Light.SegN}
\leanok
\uses{Light.Seg}
For a memory function $\mu:\mathbb{N}\to\mathbb{Z}$, a starting address $a$, and a list
$l$ of natural numbers, say that $l$ is represented in memory at $a$ when each entry is
stored as its integer cast in the corresponding consecutive cell:
$\mu(a+i)=(l[i]:\mathbb{Z})$ for every valid index $i$.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Reading a segment value]
\lean{Light.SegN.read}
\label{Light.SegN.read}
\leanok
\uses{Light.SegN}
\difficulty{3}
Let $\mu:\mathbb{N}\to\mathbb{Z}$, let $a\in\mathbb{N}$, and let $l$ be a finite list of
natural numbers such that $\mu(a+j)$ equals the integer represented by $l_j$ for every
$j<|l|$. For each $i<|l|$, $\mu(a+i)$ equals the integer represented by the $i$th entry
of $l$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Values on a natural-number segment]
\lean{Light.SegN.getElem}
\label{Light.SegN.getElem}
\leanok
\uses{Light.SegN}
\difficulty{3}
Let $\mu : \mathbb{N}\to\mathbb{Z}$, let $a\in\mathbb{N}$, and let $l$ be a finite list
of natural numbers. If the values of $\mu$ starting at $a$ agree with the entries of $l$
viewed as integers, then for every index $i<|l|$, $\mu(a+i)$ equals the integer
represented by the natural number $l_i$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Appending a value to a segment]
\lean{Light.SegN.snoc}
\label{Light.SegN.snoc}
\leanok
\uses{Light.Seg.snoc, Light.SegN}
\difficulty{3}
Let $\mu:\mathbb{N}\to\mathbb{Z}$, let $a\in\mathbb{N}$, and let $l$ be a finite list of
natural numbers such that $\mu(a+i)$ equals the integer represented by $l_i$ for every
$i<|l|$. For any natural number $x$, change $\mu$ at the single index $a+|l|$ to the
integer represented by $x$. The resulting function agrees with the list obtained by
appending $x$ to $l$ at every index of the segment starting at $a$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Extending a segment prefix by one entry]
\lean{Light.SegN.take_succ}
\label{Light.SegN.take_succ}
\leanok
\uses{Light.SegN, Light.SegN.snoc, List.take_succ_getD}
\difficulty{4}
Let $\mu:\mathbb{N}\to\mathbb{Z}$, let $a,k\in\mathbb{N}$, and let $l$ be a finite list
of natural numbers. Suppose that $\mu$ agrees with the integer cast of the list
consisting of the first $k$ entries of $l$ at every index in the segment starting at
$a$, and that $k<|l|$. Change $\mu$ at index $a+k$ to the integer represented by the
$k$th entry of $l$. The resulting function agrees with the integer cast of the first
$k+1$ entries of $l$ throughout the segment starting at $a$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Segment after dropping and taking entries]
\lean{Light.SegN.drop_take}
\label{Light.SegN.drop_take}
\leanok
\uses{Light.Seg.drop, Light.Seg.take, Light.SegN}
\difficulty{3}
Let $\mu : \mathbb{N}\to\mathbb{Z}$, let $a\in\mathbb{N}$, and let $l$ be a finite list
of natural numbers. Suppose $\mu(a+i)$ equals the integer represented by $l_i$ for every
index $i<|l|$. For any natural numbers $lo$ and $w$, the values of $\mu$ starting at
$a+lo$ agree with the natural-number entries, viewed as integers, of the list formed by
dropping the first $lo$ entries of $l$ and then taking the first $w$ entries.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Preservation of a natural segment]
\lean{Light.SegN.keep}
\label{Light.SegN.keep}
\leanok
\uses{Light.Inside, Light.SameOn, Light.Seg.keep, Light.SegN}
\difficulty{3}
Let $\mu,\mu':\mathbb{N}\to\mathbb{Z}$, let $a\in\mathbb{N}$, and let $l$ be a finite
list of natural numbers. Suppose that for every index $i<|l|$, $\mu(a+i)$ equals the
integer represented by $l_i$. If $\mu'(b)=\mu(b)$ for every $b$ with $a\le b<a+|l|$,
then for every $i<|l|$, $\mu'(a+i)$ equals the integer represented by $l_i$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Preservation outside a disjoint segment]
\lean{Light.SegN.of_sameOutside}
\label{Light.SegN.of_sameOutside}
\leanok
\uses{Light.SameOutside, Light.Seg.of_sameOutside, Light.SegN}
\difficulty{1}
Let $\mu,\mu':\mathbb{N}\to\mathbb{Z}$, let $a,b,n\in\mathbb{N}$, and let $l$ be a
finite list of natural numbers. Suppose that at every index $b+i$ for $i<|l|$, the
function $\mu$ equals the integer represented by $l_i$. Suppose also that
$\mu'(j)=\mu(j)$ whenever $j<a$ or $a+n\le j$, and that either $b+|l|\le a$ or $a+n\le
b$. Then at every index $b+i$ for $i<|l|$, the function $\mu'$ equals the integer
represented by $l_i$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{definition}[Matrix stored in memory]
\lean{Light.MatAt}
\label{Light.MatAt}
\leanok
For an $n$-by-$k$ integer matrix $A$, a memory function $\mu:\mathbb{N}\to\mathbb{Z}$,
and a starting address $a$, say that $A$ is stored at $a$ in row-major order when
$\mu(a+ik+j)=A_{ij}$ for every row $i<n$ and column $j<k$.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Agreement on a matrix interval]
\lean{Light.MatAt.congr}
\label{Light.MatAt.congr}
\leanok
\uses{Light.MatAt, Nat.mul_add_lt_mul}
\difficulty{4}
Let $n,k$ be natural numbers, let $A$ be an $n$-by-$k$ matrix of integers, and let
$\mu,\mu' : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{Z}$. Suppose that for every $i<n$ and $j<k$,
$\mu(a+ik+j)=A_{ij}$, and that $\mu'(b)=\mu(b)$ whenever $a\le b<a+nk$. Then
$\mu'(a+ik+j)=A_{ij}$ for every $i<n$ and $j<k$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Preserving a matrix on an interval]
\lean{Light.MatAt.keep}
\label{Light.MatAt.keep}
\leanok
\uses{Light.Inside, Light.MatAt, Light.MatAt.congr, Light.SameOn}
\difficulty{1}
Let $n,k$ be natural numbers, let $A$ be an $n$-by-$k$ matrix of integers, and let
$\mu,\mu' : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{Z}$. Suppose that $\mu(a+ik+j)=A_{ij}$ for every
$i<n$ and $j<k$, and that $\mu'(b)=\mu(b)$ whenever $a\le b<a+nk$. Then
$\mu'(a+ik+j)=A_{ij}$ for every $i<n$ and $j<k$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Agreement below an endpoint]
\lean{Light.MatAt.congr_below}
\label{Light.MatAt.congr_below}
\leanok
\uses{Light.MatAt, Light.MatAt.congr}
\difficulty{2}
Let $n,k,e$ be natural numbers, let $A$ be an $n$-by-$k$ matrix of integers, and let
$\mu,\mu' : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{Z}$. Suppose that $\mu(a+ik+j)=A_{ij}$ for every
$i<n$ and $j<k$, that $\mu'(x)=\mu(x)$ for every $x<e$, and that $a+nk\le e$. Then
$\mu'(a+ik+j)=A_{ij}$ for every $i<n$ and $j<k$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{definition}[Vector of indices stored in memory]
\lean{Light.VecAt}
\label{Light.VecAt}
\leanok
For an index map $I$ from $t$ positions to the natural numbers below $n$, a memory
function $\mu:\mathbb{N}\to\mathbb{Z}$, and a starting address $a$, say that $I$ is
stored at $a$ when the cell at $a+k$ contains the integer cast of the value of $I(k)$
for every position $k<t$.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Vector values from a list segment]
\lean{Light.vecAt_of_seg}
\label{Light.vecAt_of_seg}
\leanok
\uses{Light.Seg, Light.VecAt}
\difficulty{3}
Let $t,n$ be natural numbers, let $I$ map each index in $\{0,\ldots,t-1\}$ to an index
in $\{0,\ldots,n-1\}$, and let $\mu$ be an integer-valued memory function. If the
segment of $\mu$ beginning at $a$ equals the length-$t$ list whose $k$th entry is the
integer represented by $I(k)$, then for every $k<t$, the memory value at $a+k$ equals
the integer represented by $I(k)$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Preserving a represented vector]
\lean{Light.VecAt.keep}
\label{Light.VecAt.keep}
\leanok
\uses{Light.Inside, Light.SameOn, Light.VecAt}
\difficulty{3}
Let $t,n$ be natural numbers, let $I:	ext{Fin}(t)	o	ext{Fin}(n)$, and let $[?]$ and
$[?]'$ be integer-valued sequences indexed by the natural numbers. If $[?]$ represents
$I$ starting at index $a$, so that its value at $a+k$ equals the natural-number value of
$I(k)$ for every $k<t$, and the two sequences agree at every index $b$ with $a\le
b<a+t$, then $[?]'$ also represents $I$ starting at $a$.
\end{theorem}
